source: Lakoff (1993) The Contemporary Theory of Metaphor
finding: Lakoff states the theory: the locus of metaphor is thought, not language. Metaphor is a mapping from a source domain to a target domain, and everyday expressions are surface cases of it.
numbers: Evidence is listed as five types: polysemy, inference patterns, novel metaphorical language, semantic change, psycholinguistic experiments. Lakoff says he focuses on the first three as 'the most robust'.
limits: The evidence he calls most robust is linguistic generalisation by the analyst, not behaviour. Experiments are left to Gibbs. Critics later target exactly this gap.
agent_relevance: O6 rests on the claim that a good source domain carries usable inference structure into the target. The theory's own evidence for that is linguistic, so it is weak support for a measured benefit on problem solving.

source: Lakoff (1993) The Contemporary Theory of Metaphor (LOVE IS A JOURNEY worked example)
finding: A mapping is a set of ontological correspondences that carries source knowledge into the target. Lovers map to travellers, the relationship to the vehicle, common goals to destinations, difficulties to impediments. The mapping licenses inference: 'We're stuck' evokes the travel scenario (vehicle blocked; fix it, stay, or abandon it) and the scenario is re-read as a love scenario.
numbers: Four core correspondences; the 'stuck' scenario lists four alternatives for action (get it moving, stay and give up the goals, abandon the vehicle, stay with least effort).
limits: Worked by hand by the theorist. No test of whether people actually draw the mapped inferences. The set of correspondences is chosen by the analyst.
agent_relevance: This is the exact operation O6 asks the agent to perform: write the correspondence table first, then run the source-domain plan and translate the result back. The table is the checkable object.

source: Lakoff (1993) The Contemporary Theory of Metaphor (names versus mappings)
finding: Lakoff warns that the name 'LOVE IS A JOURNEY' is only a mnemonic. The mapping is the set of correspondences, and mappings are not propositions.
numbers: Not a numeric claim.
quote: metaphors are mappings, that is, sets of conceptual correspondences
limits: A definitional point; it makes the theory hard to falsify, since any list of correspondences can be called the mapping.
agent_relevance: In the scaffold, store the correspondence list as data (source item -> target item), never the slogan. Code can then check every target element has a mapped source element.

source: Lakoff (1993) The Contemporary Theory of Metaphor (Invariance Principle)
finding: Metaphorical mappings are said to preserve the image-schema structure of the source (interiors to interiors, sources to sources, goals to goals), in a way consistent with the target's own structure. It is a constraint on fixed correspondences, not an algorithm that copies and then deletes.
numbers: Hypothesis only; no data in the chapter.
limits: Stated as a hypothesis. Later work (not opened here) disputes it. Target-domain override means source inferences can be blocked where the target contradicts them.
agent_relevance: A usable guard for O6: after mapping, check that source inferences which violate target facts are dropped. This is a code-checkable constraint (G2, G3 spirit).

source: Lakoff (1993) The Contemporary Theory of Metaphor (TIME mappings)
finding: Time is mapped from space: times are things, passing of time is motion, future is in front of an observer, past behind. Two variants: observer moves through stationary times, or times move past a stationary observer.
numbers: Qualitative description of the mapping set.
limits: English-based. Cross-linguistic counterexamples exist (Aymara, see a11).
agent_relevance: Shows the template of a mapping used in experiments below. It is the one mapping with a decent experimental base, so it is the safest model of what 'a mapping that matters' looks like.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11-01) Conceptual metaphor
finding: Summary of criticisms: method was top-down from the theorists' intuitions (Kovecses 2008); metaphors may be harder, not easier, to process than literal text; once conventional, metaphors may be processed like ordinary words (Holyoak and Stamenkovic 2018); links to the body may be weaker than claimed; Pinker (2007) takes a middle position.
numbers: No numbers on the page. Mentions Dahl and Adachi 2013 (chimpanzee discrimination faster when high-rank individuals shown higher), described without statistics.
limits: Encyclopedia page, read through a summarising tool. The Murphy 1996, Keysar and Glucksberg critiques were NOT on the page and were not opened by us.
agent_relevance: Treat the theory as a source of candidate reframings, not as a proven mechanism. Conventional metaphors may do no work; only novel, structure-rich mappings are worth an O6 call.

source: Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund (2017) The psychological reality of spatio-temporal metaphors (review chapter, reporting Boroditsky 2000 and others) - Boroditsky 2000 Exp 1
finding: Boroditsky (2000, Cognition 75) built the first direct test of metaphorical structuring. Spatial scenes primed an ego-moving or object-moving frame. Then people answered the ambiguous question 'next Wednesday's meeting has been moved forward two days; what day is it now?'. Primed frame predicted the answer (ego-moving: Friday; object-moving: Monday).
numbers: 71.3% of participants answered consistently with the primed frame. Unprimed control did not differ from chance.
limits: Opened via the secondary review chapter, not the original paper (original PDF not retrievable). Primes were sentences plus pictures, so the effect may come from visual schematisation or from sentence grammar, not metaphor (chapter's critique).
agent_relevance: Space can be used to prime a way of reasoning about time. For the agent: a restated problem can change which answer is chosen on an ambiguous question, so O6 can swing answers and must be paired with a check.

source: Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund (2017) The psychological reality of spatio-temporal metaphors (review chapter, reporting Boroditsky 2000 and others) - Boroditsky 2000 Exp 2
finding: Space primed time, but time did not prime space. Control conditions (space primes space, time primes time) were above chance. Read as support for the 'weak' metaphoric structuring view: spatial schemas help think about time but are not required.
numbers: Directional result only in the chapter; exact percentages not given there.
limits: Spatial primes were pictures with captions, time primes were calendar sentences. The asymmetry could be due to unequal prime strength (chapter's critique).
agent_relevance: Asymmetry says direction matters: concrete-to-abstract reframing helps, the reverse should not be expected to. O6 should map abstract problem -> concrete source, not the opposite.

source: Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund (2017) The psychological reality of spatio-temporal metaphors (review chapter, reporting Boroditsky 2000 and others) - Boroditsky 2000 Exp 3
finding: Response-time version. People were faster to say 'true' when prime and target were in the same domain (time-time, space-space) than across domains. Spatial info sped temporal targets but not the reverse. Boroditsky took this against a 'Generic Schema' view, because time primed itself more than space primed time.
numbers: Reaction-time effect; figures not given in the chapter.
limits: Secondary report. Same prime-strength confound as Exp 2.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain restatement has a cost as well as a benefit in processing. The agent pays tokens to map and unmap; gains must beat that cost.

source: Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund (2017) The psychological reality of spatio-temporal metaphors (review chapter, reporting Boroditsky 2000 and others) - Samuel et al. frontless-box priming and Nunez et al. 2006
finding: A follow-up primed with frontless boxes (no ego) and found people still gave more 'Monday' answers than chance, for past and for future wording. Nunez, Motz and Teuscher (2006) argued the ego-moving versus time-moving split is the wrong cut and proposed Ego-RP and Time-RP framings.
numbers: Experiment 2 used 2D boxes plus a static control; primed group gave significantly more 'earlier' than 'later' for day and hour targets; control was at chance. Counts not reported in the chapter.
limits: Secondary report. Shows the Boroditsky result survives a move to a cleaner prime, but also that the theory's own two-way split was revised.
agent_relevance: The useful part of a mapping may be a reference-point structure, not the 'metaphor' label. Spell out the frame of reference explicitly when restating.

source: Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund (2017) The psychological reality of spatio-temporal metaphors (review chapter, reporting Boroditsky 2000 and others) - cross-cultural boundary conditions
finding: The English space-time mapping is not universal. Aymara speakers put the past in front (known is seen) and use gestures to match. Rothe-Wulf et al. (2014) found German, Swedish and US English speakers differ in preferred frames of reference (Swedish absolute, Germans intrinsic). Mandarin-English bilinguals use a vertical time axis. In Spain versus Morocco, front-for-future flips (de la Fuente et al. 2014).
numbers: Qualitative in the chapter; the chapter lists the groups but gives no single sample size.
limits: Secondary report. Mappings are language and culture dependent, so what counts as a 'natural' source domain varies.
agent_relevance: The best source domain depends on the audience and on the model's training mix. Do not assume one canonical mapping; try one and test it (G3).

source: Samuel, Athanasopoulos and Bylund (2017) The psychological reality of spatio-temporal metaphors (review chapter, reporting Boroditsky 2000 and others) - Casasanto and Boroditsky 2008 (line experiments)
finding: Participants judged either the length of a growing line or the time it took. Shorter lines were judged as having taken less time, but fast lines were not judged longer. Asymmetry persisted when the line did not grow and simply appeared for different durations.
numbers: Direction of the effect only in the chapter.
limits: Secondary report of a non-linguistic task. This is among the stronger behavioural pieces, because no metaphorical language is used.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that concrete magnitude is a one-way scaffold for abstract magnitude. Useful as a reason to attach concrete numbers to abstract quantities in a restatement.

source: Teuscher, McQuire, Collins and Coulson (2008) Congruity effects in time and space: behavioral and ERP measures
finding: People saw sentences about literal motion in space or metaphorical motion through time (ego-moving or object-moving), then cartoon clips whose motion direction was congruent or not. They noticed congruity for both kinds of sentence, but the brain-response (ERP) congruity effect was much smaller for time sentences than space sentences.
numbers: Exp 1: N=24 undergraduates, 72.9% correct overall, sensitivity d' = 1.7 after space sentences and 1.4 after time sentences. Exp 2 (ERP): N=12; early congruity effect for space, smaller and less robust for time. Interaction of domain by congruity F1(1,23)=4.78, p<.05.
limits: Small samples. Authors note time-sentence ERPs were noisier. The paper was set up to contrast 'system mapping' with Bowdle and Gentner's 'career of metaphor', and does not settle it.
agent_relevance: Evidence that metaphorical time sentences do evoke spatial motion, but more weakly than literal ones. A restatement is a weaker signal than the real thing; do not over-trust it.

source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011) Metaphors we think with: the role of metaphor in reasoning - Exp 1 and 2
finding: Crime described as a 'beast' versus a 'virus' in a short report changed the solutions people proposed. Beast pushed toward enforcement, virus toward reform. In Exp 2 the frame was cut to a single word ('Crime is a virus/beast ravaging the city').
numbers: Exp 1: 485 responses (30 uncodable); enforcement 74% (beast) vs 56% (virus), chi2=13.94, p<.001; overall 65% enforcement. Exp 2: N=253 US natives; enforcement 71% vs 54%, chi2=6.50, p<.05. After separating 'increase police' answers by the role participants gave police: 59% vs 37%, chi2=10.76, p<.01.
limits: Online (MTurk) samples, free-text answers coded by raters; two frames only. A later follow-up with a neutral control (a19) did not reproduce the effect.
agent_relevance: The headline founding result for 'framing changes reasoning'. Even one word shifts what plan is proposed, which means the restated problem in O6 is not neutral; it picks the plan family.

source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011) Metaphors we think with: the role of metaphor in reasoning - Exp 3 (lexical prime control)
finding: A control tested whether the effect is just word priming. People first listed a synonym for 'beast' or 'virus', then read the report without the metaphor. The effect shrank.
numbers: N=235 (124 beast, 112 virus). Congruent answers 61% with the metaphor (Exp 2) vs 50% with the lexical prime, chi2=4.23, p<.05. Police-role split did not differ between groups.
limits: A difference between significant and non-significant effects, with modest N.
agent_relevance: Metaphor as an integrated frame beats a bare keyword. In prompts, a full mapping likely beats dropping a cue word.

source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011) Metaphors we think with: the role of metaphor in reasoning - Exp 4 and 5 (information seeking, timing)
finding: The frame also changed what information people wanted next. But the effect vanished when the metaphor came at the end of the report instead of the start.
numbers: Exp 4: chose criminal-justice information 40% (beast) vs 22% (virus), chi2=5.72, p<.05. Exp 5 (frame late): 69% vs 64% social information, chi2=0.29, p=.59; differs from Exp 4, chi2=5.45, p<.05.
limits: Boundary condition: order matters. A frame only works if it comes first and can organise later text.
agent_relevance: Place the reframing at the start of a thinking step, before the facts, or it will not organise them. For O6 the mapping must precede the plan.

source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011) Metaphors we think with: the role of metaphor in reasoning - covertness and politics
finding: Almost nobody named the metaphor as influential. Republicans were less swayed than Democrats and Independents.
numbers: Metaphor named as influential: 3% (15 of 485, Exp 1), 7% (18 of 253, Exp 2), 15% (27, Exp 4), 10% (18, Exp 5). Congruent answers 63% for Democrats and Independents vs 49% for Republicans (Exp 2 and 4 pooled), chi2(1,839)=5.46, p<.05.
limits: Self-report of influence is a weak measure. The party difference is a post hoc analysis.
agent_relevance: Self-reports will not reveal reframing effects, in humans or in a model's written rationale (matches the schema rule that written reasoning is not a reliable record).

source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2013) Natural language metaphors covertly influence reasoning
finding: Follow-up with multiple-choice policy ranking. The beast frame again led to more enforcement choices, whether or not people remembered the metaphor.
numbers: First-choice enforcement 42% (beast) vs 31% (virus), N=939, chi2=12.55, p<.001. Participants who read both frames and matched policies to them: beast-matched policies were enforcement 87%, virus-matched 40%. Remembered the frame (54% congruent) vs forgot (56%), no difference, chi2=.043, p=.84, N=353. Pooled with the 2011 studies, 55-60% of answers congruent with the frame; Republicans less influenced, z=2.97.
limits: Effect size is modest (about 10 points). Pooled analysis of five experiments assumes they are comparable.
agent_relevance: Frame effects survive when the reader does not consciously retain the frame. For the agent, a reframe can bias downstream steps without being cited.

source: Steen, Reijnierse and Burgers (2014) When do natural language metaphors influence reasoning? A follow-up study to Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2013) - failed replication
finding: Four experiments (Dutch and US samples) with a no-metaphor control ('Crime is a problem') and a pre-exposure policy measure found no framing effect of beast versus virus. Pre-existing preference explained the post-exposure preference.
numbers: Final N: Exp 1 (Dutch) 253, Exp 2 (US) 259, Exp 3 252, Exp 4 1,026 after exclusions. In all four, no significant effect of metaphorical frame or of metaphorical support on policy preference. Exp 4 was sized to detect small effects.
limits: Authors do not call the original wrong: they say both the original effect and their own alternative need more research. Design differences (pre-measure, control, rank-order measure) may matter.
agent_relevance: The best-known framing result is contested. Plan on small, unstable effects and verify any benefit of O6 on our own tasks (G3) rather than citing this literature as proof.

source: Steen, Reijnierse and Burgers (2014) When do natural language metaphors influence reasoning? A follow-up study to Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2013) - design points
finding: Authors argue the original design left room for alternative explanations: no neutral control, no baseline preference measure, possible demand effects from the metaphor-memory question. They add a 'problem' control and measure preferences before and after reading.
numbers: Planned about 300 completed surveys (about 50 per cell) in Exp 1 to 3 and about 1,200 in Exp 4; time-on-page exclusions (under 5 s or over 60 s).
limits: Post hoc power analysis reported; details not copied in full.
agent_relevance: When we test O6 reframing on our tasks, include a no-reframe control and a pre-measure, as this paper shows is needed.

source: Durgin et al. (2026) A downside of conceptual metaphor: metaphoric alignments of black and white (six experiments)
finding: A black-white color IAT gave as strong bias as the race IAT. Race and color IAT scores correlate as strongly as two race IATs do, in White and in Black participants. The bias tracks figurative meanings of colors (good-evil), not literal color preference. Authors read this as the metaphor mapping contributing to race IAT performance.
numbers: Exp 2 (200 White participants): mean IAT 0.41 (race, d=1.12), 0.45 (color chess pieces, d=1.44); color-race r=.30 [.11,.47], race-race r=.31 [.12,.47]. Race IAT test-retest about .4 (Gawronski 2017 cited).
limits: IAT validity itself is disputed; the authors defend it. Online samples. Only fulltext read via the PMC XML; some experiments not read in detail.
agent_relevance: A new 2026 data point that conceptual metaphors can leak a value judgement into an unrelated target. A source domain carries its valence with it, so an O6 restatement can import a bias.

source: No evidence for the influence of head-heart conceptual metaphor on moral decision making and personality (J Gen Psychol, 2025)
finding: A failed replication of embodied-metaphor effects. Pointing to the heart versus the head did not change moral dilemma answers. Self-location as heart or head did not predict affect intensity, femininity or intimacy.
numbers: Exps 1a and 1b: 203 participants. Exps 2a and 2b: 304 participants (Hong Kong and mainland China). Failed to replicate; Bayesian analyses supported no effect.
limits: Abstract only, from Europe PMC. Full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Embodied-metaphor effects in social psychology often fail in high-powered replication; do not borrow their effect sizes.

source: Ichien, Stamenkovic and Holyoak (2023) Large language model displays emergent ability to interpret novel literary metaphors - Fig-QA
finding: GPT-4 zero-shot on the Fig-QA figurative benchmark came close to humans and beat earlier models.
numbers: GPT-4 91.27%; human 94.42% (95.39% excluding low-confidence items); GPT-3 Davinci zero-shot 68.41%; fine-tuned RoBERTa 90.32%. About 3.35% of GPT-4 outputs gave no unambiguous answer.
limits: Fig-QA may overlap with training data (authors say so). Hence the next two studies use unpublished material.
agent_relevance: A frontier model recognises figurative meaning at near-human accuracy, so the 'understand the metaphor' step of O6 is usually not the bottleneck.

source: Ichien, Stamenkovic and Holyoak (2023) Large language model displays emergent ability to interpret novel literary metaphors - novel Serbian poetry metaphors
finding: 55 novel metaphors from Serbian poems, translated and shown in canonical and reversed (source/target swapped) form. Blind human judges scored GPT-4's interpretations above those of college students. Both humans and GPT-4 often restored the canonical meaning when given the reversed form.
numbers: 110 items; humans gave about 19.5 responses per item (range 12 to 27); 235 Serbian raters normed the originals. Source effect b=.194, z=2.01, p=.045 (GPT-4 higher); metaphor form b=.383, z=7.50, p<.001. Reversed metaphors restored to canonical meaning 56% (GPT-4) vs 50% (humans); item-level point-biserial r=0.79 across 55 items.
limits: Marginal p-value. Human comparison group was college students, not poets or critics. GPT-4 may have seen some of the translations online (34.5% had pre-2022 web matches; no interaction found).
agent_relevance: LLMs follow the same pragmatic direction rule as people (source to target). Good sign for a source-to-target mapping step.

source: Ichien, Stamenkovic and Holyoak (2023) Large language model displays emergent ability to interpret novel literary metaphors - poems judged by a critic
finding: GPT-4 interpreted entire new English poems. A professional critic, blind to the source, graded each interpretation from A (excellent) to E (poor) and rated the first seven as excellent.
numbers: Seven of the first interpretations rated excellent; full grades are in the paper's appendix (not extracted here).
limits: Single critic; few poems; no human baseline for this study.
agent_relevance: Interpretation is strong. The weakness will be in applying mappings to solve, not in reading them.

source: Prystawski, Thibodeau, Potts and Goodman (2022) Psychologically-informed chain-of-thought prompts for metaphor understanding in large language models
finding: Paraphrase choice for metaphors on the Katz corpus. GPT-3 text-davinci-002 was already strong with no rationale; the small Curie model was at chance. Rationales built from cognitive theories (question under discussion, similarity) helped Curie, but not much for DaVinci.
numbers: Mean appropriateness (1 to 4; chance 2.5), DaVinci: options-only 2.73, no rationale 3.71, non-explanation 3.58, subject-object 3.84, QUD 3.74, similarity 3.68. Curie: no rationale at chance (p=.97); QUD significantly above chance (p=.005), similarity p=.02, but QUD vs no-rationale not significant (beta=.41, CI -.02 to .84). Parse failures: Curie 47 of 150 with subject-object prompts. Familiarity effect on DaVinci beta=.36 [.01,.73] only without rationales. Corpus: 230 non-literary and 50 literary metaphors; 150 test items.
limits: Old models (2022). Single corpus. Differences among the DaVinci prompts are small and overlap in their intervals.
agent_relevance: Structured, theory-based reasoning scaffolds help weak models and add little to strong ones. This supports adding O6 only for tasks where the base model fails.

source: Tong, Choenni, Lewis and Shutova (2024) Metaphor Understanding Challenge Dataset for LLMs (MUNCH)
finding: A dataset built from Conceptual Metaphor Theory: apt paraphrases reflect the target domain, inapt ones reflect the literal source sense. Models often fail to tell them apart.
numbers: 10k+ paraphrases; 3k sentences (2,953 used for generation); 1,492 triples for 728 sentences (1,072 apt+inapt, 375 two inapt, 45 two apt). Judgement accuracy of LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-30B and GPT-3.5 was below the 0.25 random baseline in most conditions (e.g. GPT-3.5 0.16 to 0.23, LLaMA-30B 0.14 to 0.27). Generation MRR: LLaMA-13B .33, LLaMA-30B .47, GPT-3.5 .54; recall@5 .22, .28, .32.
limits: Older models (LLaMA-1, GPT-3.5); GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 not tested (authors note). Below-chance scores suggest prompt trouble as well as model trouble.
agent_relevance: Models confuse the source sense and the target sense. For O6, the mapping step must name which sense is intended and a check should reject outputs that stay in the literal source meaning.

source: Aghazadeh, Fayyaz and Yaghoobzadeh (2022) Metaphors in pre-trained language models: probing and generalization across datasets and languages
finding: Probing BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA shows metaphoricity information is encoded, mostly in middle layers, and transfers across four languages (English, Spanish, Russian, Farsi) and four datasets when annotation is consistent.
numbers: Edge-probing accuracy on LCC (en): random-init baseline 74.86; BERT 88.25; RoBERTa 88.06; ELECTRA 89.30 (average of three runs; row order read from the table text). TroFi about 68 vs 65.92 baseline (small gap). VUA POS 80 to 83 vs 65.92 baseline. MDL compression peaks at layers about 3 to 6.
limits: Base-size models only. Detection of 'is it metaphoric' is not the same as mapping source to target. Gains on TroFi are small. Table layout was flattened by the PDF extractor, so row labels are inferred.
agent_relevance: Models carry metaphor signal internally, but that signal is detection, not structured mapping. Do not assume the model has an explicit mapping table to read out.

source: Stowe, Chakrabarty, Peng, Muresan and Gurevych (2021) Metaphor generation with conceptual mappings
finding: First computational model that uses conceptual mappings to steer metaphor generation. CM-Lex shifts verbs between FrameNet frames; CM-BART is a BART model conditioned on a source and target domain pair. Unconditioned systems write fine metaphors but ignore the intended source domain.
numbers: Human ratings (1 to 4; 3 experts), gold mappings, metaphoricity / source evocation: MetMask 2.27/1.60; MERMAID 2.56/2.12; CM-Lex 2.34/2.43; CM-BART 2.72/2.87. Unseen mappings: CM-BART 2.41/2.01 vs CM-Lex 1.58/1.14. Automatic: exact match with gold 29.3% (CM-BART) vs 13.3% (MERMAID). Annotator agreement only .50 (metaphoricity) and .37 (source domain).
limits: Agreement is low. Verb-replacement metaphors only. Pre-LLM models.
agent_relevance: A hand-built mapping encoder is a working computational form of CMT. Shows that giving the model the source-target pair explicitly raises source-domain fidelity, which supports an explicit mapping slot in O6.

source: Kramer (2025) Conceptual Metaphor Theory as a prompting paradigm for large language models
finding: A system message tells the model to read abstract targets through concrete sources before reasoning. On 100 self-made problems in four task groups (metaphor interpretation, domain-specific reasoning, explanation, reading comprehension) the author reports CMT prompting matched or beat baselines.
numbers: Four small models only: Llama3.2 3B, Phi3 3.8B, Gemma2 2B, Mistral 7B. Judge: Llama3.3 70B. Results shown only in bar charts; no numbers in the text. Gains vary by model; Mistral and Gemma are 'inconsistent' on reading comprehension.
limits: Weak evidence: self-built benchmark, LLM judge, tiny models, no reported statistics, a single author. Cannot be used as proof that O6 helps.
agent_relevance: The only paper found that directly tests a source-target prompt as a reasoning aid, and it is too weak to rely on. Our own test of O6 is needed.

source: Ye, Wang, Chao and Wong (2025/2026) Probing semantic alignment, lexical invariance and syntactic influence in LLM metaphor processing (arXiv 2510.04120 v2)
finding: LLMs do well on metaphor tasks but the diagnostics show semantic drift from the intended attribute, stable lexical anchors that may favour conventional metaphors and bias novel ones, and detection that is sensitive to syntax shuffling.
numbers: Multiple-choice validation on attribute-matched options was near chance: 50.89, 51.69, 50.77, 50.92, 50.85, 47.31, 46.04 across seven models (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o3-mini, R1, LLaMA-3.1-8B; model-to-number order read from a flattened table). LLaMA-3.1-8B detection stayed near 50% under all perturbations.
limits: Fine-grained polarity or intensity options make the test very hard; authors say discrete accuracy hides how far outputs drift. Table order inferred.
agent_relevance: Strong benchmark scores can hide a poor grasp of which attribute is mapped. The mapping step needs an explicit 'which attribute carries over' field and a check.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Metaphor-induced algorithmic steering: cross-domain procedural transfer in LLM code generation
finding: Benign instructions written as metaphors (e.g. a clinical review procedure) made code models pick less efficient algorithms (full scans, repeated rebuilds) more often than literal instructions. Hidden states shift toward low-efficiency procedural prototypes.
numbers: Steering success per sample / per task: Qwen 23.3% / 41.1% (metaphor) vs 9.6% / 17.8% (literal); DeepSeek 34.5% / 43.8% vs 4.4% / 8.2%; Gemma 23.6% / 28.6% vs 2.9% / 3.9%. Manual audit: metaphor-implied procedure visible in code for 90.9% (Gemma), 78.4% (Qwen), 21.9% (DeepSeek) of successful cases. Detector macro F1 86.6% (instruction form, 270 skills) and 90.3% (impact).
limits: Adversarial framing built by an iterative generator on APPS and BIRD-SQL; success is defined as lowered efficiency, so it measures a harm. Not a test of benefit.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for a risk in O6: a source-domain restatement can import the source's procedure into the target task even when unwanted. Require the agent to list which source steps do NOT transfer.
